name: Dynamic leverage
tagline: 30% TQQQ core + 70% 65%-vol-target sleeve, with the winner's armed 4% minute stop.
summary: On risk-on sessions (QQQ prior close above its 165-day SMA), hold a 30% permanent TQQQ core and put the other 70% into an inverse-vol TQQQ sleeve that targets 65% annualised 20-day volatility, with BIL as the residual; on risk-off sessions hold 100% BIL. The round-1 winner's armed 4% minute stop is applied on top. At 1 bp it returns 57.05% / 41.32% over 10 years and 50.12% / 30.16% over 5 years, versus the winner's 58.80% / 44.56% and 49.88% / 33.49%.
decision_process: At each session's close, compute QQQ's 165-day SMA and TQQQ's 20-day realised volatility from daily closes; both are known before the next open. If QQQ's prior close is below its 165-day SMA, target 100% BIL. Otherwise target w_TQQQ = 0.30 + 0.70 × min(1, 0.65 / vol20), with BIL for the remainder; the 2% trade band suppresses small daily resizes. These daily targets are set from the prior close and fill at the next bar's open (09:31 for the first bar of the session). Intraday, on a risk-on day, the 4% stop is armed only when QQQ's first-minute close is below its prior 20-day SMA × 1.01; if armed and TQQQ's 1-minute close falls 4% below the session open, the whole book is sold at the next minute's open and held in BIL for the rest of the session and overnight. No same-bar fills.
rules: Regime: if QQQ's prior daily close is above its 165-day SMA, the next session is risk-on; otherwise hold 100% BIL.

Risk-on sizing: w_TQQQ = 0.30 + 0.70 × min(1, 0.65 / vol20), where vol20 is the annualised 20-day standard deviation of TQQQ daily close-to-close log returns through the prior close; the remainder is BIL.
Long-only, weights sum to at most 1, and TQQQ weight never exceeds 100% (no leverage beyond TQQQ's embedded 3×).
Arm the stop only on a risk-on day when QQQ's first-minute close is below its prior 20-day SMA × 1.01.

If armed and TQQQ's 1-minute close is 4% below the session open, sell the whole book at the next minute's open and stay in BIL for the rest of the session and the following night; re-enter next session if the regime is still on.
Daily targets are set from data through the prior close and fill at the next bar's open; the 2% rebalance band applies.
verdict: Meets the round-2 'lower drawdown with CAGR within 2 pp' test on both windows and at 1, 5 and 10 bp: 10y 57.05% / 41.32% vs the winner's 58.80% / 44.56% (CAGR −1.75 pp, DD −3.24 pp), 5y 50.12% / 30.16% is strict dominance. Calmar improves from 1.32 to 1.38 (10y) and 1.49 to 1.66 (5y). Main caveat: the 10y pass has only a 0.25 pp cushion (57.05% vs the 56.80% floor; the 20% core neighbour is 56.71% and misses), and rolling return wins are 22/27 vs the winner's 23/27, so the consistency gain is in drawdown, not return. The CAGR give-up is concentrated in the 2020 V-recovery.

sources.idea: Scale exposure inversely to recent realised variance; volatility-managed equity portfolios raise Sharpe because volatility changes are not matched one-for-one by expected-return changes.
sources.evidence: The inverse-vol TQQQ sleeve (65% target, 20-day window) is a capped implementation of their volatility-managed portfolio. Their mechanism is the reason the strategy cuts exposure when TQQQ vol is high rather than after a loss.

sources.idea: Volatility targeting improves Sharpe and reduces the severity of left-tail events and maximum drawdowns; a slow, broad realised-vol estimator is preferred to a fast timing signal.
sources.source: Harvey, Hoyle, Korgaonkar, Rattray, Sargaison & Van Hemert (2018) / The Impact of Volatility Targeting
sources.evidence: Supports the 20-day daily-close estimator and the claim that the main benefit is drawdown/tail reduction, not higher average return. The paper also documents the cost of targeting too aggressively, which motivated the 30% permanent core.

sources.idea: Volatility-managed portfolios often fail out of sample because of estimation instability, so the adjustment should be tempered rather than an all-or-nothing vol switch.
sources.source: Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020) / On the Performance of Volatility-Managed Portfolios
sources.evidence: This is the main reason the implementation keeps a 30% permanent TQQQ core and applies the vol target only to the other 70%. A pure 65% target has the best Calmar but gives up 2.66 pp of 10y CAGR, outside the 2 pp band.

sources.idea: Conditional volatility targeting can enhance Sharpe and reduce drawdowns and tail risk with low turnover.
sources.source: Bongaerts, Kang & van Dijk (2020) / Conditional Volatility Targeting
sources.evidence: Supports a conditional/tempered vol-target rule instead of a constant leverage; the paper's low-turnover finding is consistent with the 2% band and ~93.9% average TQQQ target weight here.

sources.idea: For excess mean μ and variance σ², the growth-optimal fraction is f* = μ/σ²; full Kelly is too aggressive under parameter uncertainty, so fractional Kelly is the practical choice.
sources.source: Thorp (2006) / The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market
sources.evidence: The 30/70 blend is a shrunk inverse-vol rule in the same spirit as fractional Kelly: keep a fixed core, apply a fraction of the vol-target adjustment. The literal daily Kelly formula was tested separately and rejected (see rejected_sources).

sources.idea: A daily-reset 3× ETF's multi-day log return is approximately 3× the index log return minus 3 × the sum of squared daily returns; volatility drag and path dependence grow with realised variance.
sources.source: Cheng & Madhavan (2009) / The Dynamics of Leveraged and Inverse Exchange-Traded Funds
sources.evidence: Explains why TQQQ exposure should be reduced when its own realised volatility is high: the drag term is proportional to Σr², which is exactly the state variable used in the throttle.

sources.idea: TQQQ seeks 3× the daily index return, not 3× over longer periods; volatile markets can produce multi-day returns far from 3× and large drawdowns.
sources.source: ProShares / TQQQ UltraPro QQQ Summary Prospectus
sources.evidence: Primary-document confirmation of the daily-reset and holding-period risk that the vol throttle is designed to manage.

sources.idea: A long moving-average trend filter (10-month/200-day style) keeps most of the equity return with much smaller drawdowns.
sources.source: Faber (2007) / A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation
sources.evidence: The 165-day QQQ SMA regime is inherited from the round-1 winner, which follows this trend-filter literature; this strategy does not re-optimise the SMA.

sources.idea: Leveraged equity can be held while the index is above its long average and moved to T-bills below it.
sources.source: Gayed & Bilello (2016) / Leverage for the Long Run
sources.evidence: Supports the regime-plus-leverage structure inherited from the winner; the round-2 contribution is only the sizing overlay.

sources.idea: Volatility targeting reduces drawdowns; average exposure falls when volatility is high.
sources.source: Man Group / The Impact of Volatility Targeting
sources.evidence: Practitioner summary of the same mechanism; used as a cross-check, not as the primary evidence.

sources.idea: The exact 30% core, 65% target, 20-day window and 2% band were chosen from the local 1-minute QQQ/TQQQ/BIL parameter surface.
sources.evidence: The surface is monotone in the target (45/55/65/80% gives 10y CAGR 49.50/53.40/56.14/58.13% and DD 32.21/36.51/39.92/43.31%). The 30% core is the round middle of a flat 20–40% plateau (10y CAGR 56.71/57.05/57.31%, DD 40.77/41.32/41.82%); it was not fitted to a single cell.

sources.idea: The 165-day QQQ SMA regime, the armed 4% minute stop and the benchmark metrics are inherited from the round-1 winner.
sources.evidence: Winner: 58.80% / 44.56% (10y) and 49.88% / 33.49% (5y) at 1 bp. This strategy is an overlay on that exact rule set; the stop and regime were not changed.

rejected_sources.source: Grossman & Zhou (1993) / Optimal Investment Strategies for Controlling Drawdowns
rejected_sources.why_rejected: The implied drawdown-from-high exposure rule was tested as a 60-day drawdown throttle (w = 1 − 0.5×|DD60|, floor 25%): 10y 57.40% / 43.56%, 5y 48.70% / 32.99%, Calmar 1.32 / 1.48 versus the primary's 1.38 / 1.66. It cuts after the loss has happened and misses the rebound, so it is not used.

The practical 'exposure decreasing in drawdown' rule is the same mechanism as the Grossman–Zhou test above. Tested and rejected: no Calmar gain, and the 10y drawdown falls only from 44.56% to 43.56% while CAGR falls 1.4 pp.

rejected_sources.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) / Time Series Momentum
rejected_sources.why_rejected: Trend-strength scaling was tested as w = 0.5 + 0.5×trend/4% (floor 50%, where trend = QQQ/SMA165 − 1): 10y 53.35% / 42.39%, 5y 43.46% / 33.46%. It is procyclical — smallest exactly at recovery starts (2019, 2020, 2023) — and lost 2–12 pp of CAGR with little drawdown benefit.

rejected_sources.source: Thorp (2006) / Kelly criterion, direct daily implementation
rejected_sources.why_rejected: The literal fractional Kelly rule 0.5×μ60/σ²60, capped at 100%, was tested: 10y 25.35% / 45.38%, 5y 18.03% / 39.46%. Daily μ and σ² estimates are too noisy and imply only 20–30% exposure; full Kelly is worse. Kelly survives only as the conceptual basis for the shrunk 30/70 blend, not as a direct sizing formula.

rejected_sources.source: Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012) / Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity
rejected_sources.why_rejected: Listed on the current web page but not a source for this strategy. It is a leverage-aversion/risk-parity paper, was not used to design the vol-target throttle, and was not tested here. Remove it from the paper list rather than presenting it as provenance.

corrections: The page omits the 165-day QQQ SMA regime. It must state: if QQQ's prior close is below its 165-day SMA, the next session is 100% BIL; the volatility sizing applies only on risk-on sessions. As written, 'residual BIL' implies an always-invested book, which is wrong.

The decision text 'Signals use only data through the current bar' is inaccurate. Daily signals use the prior session's close (regime and 20-day vol); only the stop uses the current 1-minute close; every target fills at the next bar's open (09:31 for the first bar). Truncation at 2022-01-03 leaves all prior weights bit-identical.

The rules omit the stop's arm condition and holding period: it is armed only when QQQ's first-minute close is below its prior 20-day SMA × 1.01, and after a 4% stop the book stays in BIL for the rest of the session and the following night, re-entering next session if the regime is on.

The '70% sleeve at a 65% volatility target' phrasing should be written as w_TQQQ = 0.30 + 0.70 × min(1, 0.65/vol20) with BIL residual. The 70% is the weight on the vol-target signal, not a sleeve that is always 70% invested; when vol > 65% part of the sleeve is in BIL.

Paper list: remove Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012) — it is not a source and was not tested. Replace the four generic 'doi.org' labels with their citations (Moreira–Muir DOI, Harvey JPM DOI, Cederburg DOI, Bongaerts DOI) and add Cheng & Madhavan (2009) for the 3× volatility-drag premise. Grossman–Zhou, Thorp and Moskowitz et al. belong in tested/rejected, not inspiration.

The verdict should include the thin 10y margin: 57.05% vs the 56.80% floor is a 0.25 pp cushion, and the 20% core neighbour is 56.71% and misses. Rolling return wins are 22/27 vs the winner's 23/27, so the consistency gain is drawdown, not return.
